planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Hagley Hybrid flowers entirely on new growth, so it tolerates a hard cutback to about a foot from the ground in late winter without sacrificing bloom.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis, obelisk, or fence, since this cultivar's pale flower color holds up well even in strong light compared to darker-striped types. Bred in England and named for Hagley Hall, this cultivar produces abundant medium-sized flowers in a soft shell-pink to mauve-pink shade with contrasting golden-brown anthers, blooming continuously from early summer well into fall. Because flowers form only on the current season's growth, cut the entire vine back hard each late winter to keep it compact, floriferous, and free of the tangled bare growth that untrimmed vines develop over the years. Its long bloom season and modest ultimate size make it a good choice for a large container or a smaller trellis where a rampant montana-type clematis would be unsuitable.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; General Sikorski blooms on old wood in early summer with a lighter rebloom on new growth, so limit late-winter pruning to removing dead or weak stems rather than a hard cutback.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a sturdy trellis or fence. Bred by the Polish hybridizer Brother Stefan Franczak and named for the Polish general and wartime prime minister, this cultivar bears large, rounded flowers in a rich mid-blue with a subtle darker central bar and cream-colored anthers, opening in early summer and often continuing sporadically into fall. Because the main flush forms on stems carried over from the prior season, prune only lightly in late winter to remove dead or damaged growth, preserving the older wood responsible for the heaviest bloom. It is a vigorous, reliable grower that has become a widely available garden favorite for its clean, saturated blue color.

common_name: Rebecca Clematis (Velvety Deep Red Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Rebecca flowers on new growth through the season, so it can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter to keep it compact and full.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis, obelisk, or large container support. Bred by Raymond Evison and named in memory of a family member, this cultivar produces velvety, deep crimson-red flowers with a lighter central bar and pale yellow anthers, held on a relatively compact vine that blooms repeatedly from early summer through fall on new growth. Its manageable mature size makes it well suited to a patio container or small trellis where larger montana- or viticella-type clematis would quickly outgrow the space. Cut the entire vine back hard in late winter to encourage a full flush of vigorous new flowering stems.

common_name: Rubens Clematis Montana (Bronze-Foliage Pink Spring Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Rubens is a vigorous spring-blooming Clematis montana selection that needs a very sturdy, large support and should be pruned only right after flowering.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a large, sturdy support such as a pergola, wall, or mature tree. One of the oldest and most widely planted Clematis montana selections, Rubens emerges with bronze-purple young foliage that matures to green, setting off a single overwhelming spring flush of soft rose-pink, faintly vanilla-scented flowers with contrasting yellow anthers. It flowers on the previous year's growth, so any pruning needed to control its considerable size should be done immediately after the spring bloom rather than in winter or early spring, which would remove that year's flowers. Give it plenty of room, since a mature vine easily covers a large wall, fence, or tree canopy.

common_name: Aunt Dee Wisteria (Deep Purple Repeat-Blooming Kentucky Wisteria)

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, pergola, or arbor capable of supporting the mature vine's substantial weight.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun on a sturdy support structure; Aunt Dee is a named selection of Wisteria macrostachya, the well-behaved native Kentucky wisteria, prized for dense racemes of fragrant, deep purple flowers that open earlier in spring than many other wisteria and are followed by a lighter repeat bloom in summer. Like other Kentucky wisteria selections it twines clockwise, reaches flowering size faster than seed-grown plants, and grows far less aggressively than the Asian species that have naturalized and become invasive across much of the southeastern United States. It requires only annual pruning to control size and shape rather than the constant vigilance needed to contain Chinese or Japanese wisteria, making it a better choice where a well-mannered, non-invasive vine is wanted.

common_name: Royal Purple Wisteria (Deep Violet-Purple Japanese Wisteria)

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on an extremely sturdy pergola or arbor built to carry the mature vine's substantial weight.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on an extremely sturdy support structure, since mature vines become massive and heavy over time. Royal Purple bears dense, fragrant racemes of deep violet-purple flowers, richer and darker than the lavender-blue of the common species, opening in late spring after the leaves emerge. Like other Japanese wisteria cultivars it twines clockwise and grows vigorously, requiring firm annual pruning both in summer to control rampant new growth and in late winter to encourage flower bud formation; it is classified as invasive in parts of the eastern and southeastern United States, where it can escape cultivation and smother trees, so gardeners in those regions may prefer a native Wisteria frutescens or W. macrostachya cultivar instead. Give it many years and a genuinely strong, permanent structure to reach its full flowering potential.
